1415.title: The Holy See
1415.hook: the pope's office and the tiny state that protects it
1415.howItsDone: Catholics pray for the pope by name in the Eucharistic Prayer at Mass, and some pray for the pope's intentions, often with an Our Father and a Hail Mary. Nations send ambassadors to the Holy See, and the Holy See sends nuncios to them.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the diocese: a portion of the people of God, gathered around the bishop's chair. Your line was the local church.

When a new ambassador arrives in Rome to represent a country to the pope, the paperwork doesn't say Vatican City. It names something else: the Holy See. Two names, one small patch of ground beside the Tiber, and they aren't the same thing. One is a state, with walls, gardens, a post office and stamps. The other isn't a place at all. It's an office, and the state exists to keep it free.
screen: `AN AMBASSADOR ARRIVES IN ROME.` → `NOT VATICAN CITY, THE HOLY SEE.` → `A STATE AND AN OFFICE.`

segments.voice: Back on day six hundred fifty-three, the Chair of Saint Peter: a feast of Peter's teaching office, not a piece of furniture. See is an old word for a seat, and yesterday you met one: the bishop's chair in the cathedral. Every bishop has a see. The pope is the bishop of Rome, so his see is the see of Rome, which Catholics call the Holy See, or the Apostolic See. What does the name cover? The Code of Canon Law says it means the pope himself, and also the offices that help him govern the Church, like the Secretariat of State. So when the Holy See signs an agreement or sends a nuncio abroad, it's the pope's office acting, not a city. Why give this see its weight? Catholics point to Jesus's words to Peter in Matthew's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims: "And I say to thee: That thou art Peter; and upon this rock I will build my church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it." Catholic tradition holds that Peter's ministry continues in the bishops of Rome, where Peter died. Orthodox Christians honor the bishop of Rome in their own way, and Protestant churches read the verse in other ways; the Catholic reading is the one this path follows. Last, the tiny state. Vatican City is a small sovereign territory, and its point is protection: a pope who answered to a government could be pressured by it. The state is the shell; the see is what it carries, like a backpack and the letter inside it.
screen: `A SEE IS A SEAT.` · `THE POPE AND HIS OFFICES.` · `UPON THIS ROCK.` · `THE STATE PROTECTS THE SEE.` · then, large: `THOU ART PETER.`

segments.voice: Think of how much passes across one desk in a single day: letters from bishops, news of wars and floods, decisions about people far away. If you pray, pray for the pope and those who work alongside him; some Catholics pray an Our Father and a Hail Mary for the pope's intentions, or simply hold him in silence. If you don't pray, hold in mind anyone who carries heavy decisions for many people, and wish them wisdom.
The Holy See. The pope's office as bishop of Rome, with the offices that serve him, protected by a small state. Today's word.
Your line: the see of Peter. A seat, an office, a letter carried in a very small backpack. Back tomorrow, same hill.

1416.title: Canon law
1416.hook: the Church's law ends by saying its highest rule is the salvation of souls
1416.howItsDone: Catholic dioceses have canon lawyers and church courts, called tribunals, that apply canon law, including in marriage cases. Priests and bishops study it as part of their training.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Holy See: the pope's office, a seat rather than a city, protected by a tiny state. Your line was the see of Peter.

Skip to the last page of a rulebook and you'll usually find an index, a clause about definitions, or nothing at all. The Catholic Church's book of law is thick, numbered from start to finish, full of rules about marriages, parishes, property and courts. A reader who skips to the end finds a short canon about moving a parish priest from one parish to another. And in its very last words, the whole book says what all the other rules are for.
screen: `THE LAST PAGE OF A RULEBOOK.` → `MARRIAGES, PARISHES, PROPERTY, COURTS.` → `THE LAST WORDS SAY WHAT IT'S FOR.`

segments.voice: Canon law is the Church's own law, the rules by which the Catholic Church orders its life: who may be ordained, how a parish is set up, how a marriage case is heard. This week has leaned on it again and again, for secular institutes, the parish, the diocese and the Holy See. The Latin Church has its Code of Canon Law; the Eastern Catholic Churches have their own code. What canon law is not: the faith itself, or a list of everything holy. It's more like the plumbing and wiring of a house: unglamorous, mostly unnoticed, and badly missed when it fails. Now, that last canon. It deals with a hard moment: a bishop needs to transfer a pastor who doesn't want to go. The canon tells the bishop to act with fairness, what canonists call canonical equity, and to keep before his eyes the salvation of souls, which, it says, must always be the supreme law in the Church. In Latin, the key words are salus animarum. So the book ends not with a penalty but with a purpose, and every rule in it is meant to be read in that light. Jesus describes himself in John's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims: "I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd giveth his life for his sheep." Canon law is the Church's attempt to organize shepherding, and its final line reminds every bishop, priest and judge that the sheep are the point.
screen: `THE CHURCH'S OWN LAW.` · `PLUMBING AND WIRING, NOT THE HOUSE.` · `THE LAST CANON: THE SALVATION OF SOULS.` · `THE SHEEP ARE THE POINT.` · then, large: `THE SUPREME LAW IN THE CHURCH.`

segments.voice: Let the last canon's idea come slowly: fairness, and before your eyes, the salvation of souls, the supreme law. Then think of one rule you keep at home or at work, and ask what it's for, and whether it still serves the people it was made for. If you pray, bring that rule and the people it touches to God; if you don't, sit with the question.

1417.title: Spiritual ecumenism
1417.hook: Vatican II calls prayer the soul of Christian unity
1417.howItsDone: Catholics pray for Christian unity at Mass and in private, and join other Christians in shared services of prayer, especially during the week of prayer for Christian unity.

segments.voice: Yesterday, canon law, and its last line: the salvation of souls is the supreme law. Your line was for souls.

On the night before he died, Jesus prayed out loud for the people who would come after his friends, people he would never meet. John's Gospel keeps the words. He didn't ask that they be clever, or successful, or even safe. He asked that they be one. Christians have argued, split and sometimes fought ever since. And when the Catholic Church sat down at the Second Vatican Council to ask how to mend those splits, it put something before the meetings and the documents.
screen: `THE NIGHT BEFORE HE DIED.` → `HE ASKED THAT THEY BE ONE.` → `SOMETHING BEFORE THE MEETINGS.`

segments.voice: You met this prayer on day five hundred twenty-five, and the Week of Prayer for Christian Unity on day six hundred forty-seven. In the Douay-Rheims, John chapter seventeen: "That they all may be one, as thou, Father, in me, and I in thee; that they also may be one in us; that the world may believe that thou hast sent me." Notice the last clause. Unity isn't only about Christians getting along; it's tied to whether the world can believe at all. Ecumenism is the work of Christians from divided churches seeking the unity Jesus prayed for. It includes theologians in dialogue and joint statements, and you'll meet some of those in the coming days. But the council's decree on ecumenism put something first. It says that a change of heart and holiness of life, together with public and private prayer for the unity of Christians, should be seen as the soul of the whole ecumenical movement. And it gives this a name: spiritual ecumenism. The soul, the decree says: not decoration on top of the real work, but what makes the work alive. The same decree says Catholics may, in certain circumstances, join in prayer with other Christians for unity. That's the week of prayer, when churches that can't yet share one altar still share one prayer. In the council's picture, changed hearts are the soul of the work, and the documents serve them. A dialogue between people who have prayed together starts from a different place than a negotiation between strangers.
screen: `THAT THEY ALL MAY BE ONE.` · `CHRISTIANS SEEKING UNITY.` · `PRAYER IS THE SOUL OF IT.` · `HEARTS FIRST, THEN DOCUMENTS.` · then, large: `THAT THE WORLD MAY BELIEVE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one Christian you know from a different church, a Baptist neighbor, an Orthodox coworker, a cousin whose church has a band, and hold their face for a moment. If you pray, pray for them and for unity in the words of John seventeen: that they all may be one. If you don't pray, hold them in mind with goodwill.

Your line: prayer first. Hearts first, and then the documents. Until tomorrow.

1418.title: Anglicans and Catholics
1418.hook: decades of dialogue and shared prayer
1418.howItsDone: Catholics and Anglicans continue an official theological dialogue through a joint international commission, and their leaders meet and pray together. Locally, parishes sometimes share services of prayer for Christian unity.

segments.voice: Yesterday, spiritual ecumenism: prayer and a change of heart, the soul of Christian unity. Your line was prayer first.

A pope and an archbishop of Canterbury meet in Rome. Their churches have been apart a long time, with plenty of bitter history between them. They pray together and sign a declaration. Then, the story goes, Pope Paul the Sixth does something no document asked for. He takes the ring from his own finger and slips it onto the hand of Archbishop Michael Ramsey. Ramsey, by the usual telling, wore it for the rest of his life.
screen: `A POPE AND AN ARCHBISHOP IN ROME.` → `A RING FROM HIS OWN FINGER.` → `WORN FOR THE REST OF HIS LIFE.`

segments.voice: Who are Anglicans? The Church of England, and the churches around the world in communion with the archbishop of Canterbury, form the Anglican Communion. Its worship grew from the English Reformation, and Catholics and Anglicans have long disagreed about the papacy, the ordained ministry and more. Those disagreements are real, and neither side pretends otherwise. After that meeting in Rome, the two churches set up a joint commission of theologians, known by its initials as ARCIC. It has worked through hard questions, the Eucharist, ministry, authority, Mary, and published agreed statements, saying plainly where they agree and where they still don't. And look at what they already share. Anglican evening prayer, in the Book of Common Prayer, ends with collects, short prayers, and tradition traces one of them to an older Latin evening prayer. In the 1662 book it reads: "Lighten our darkness, we beseech thee, O Lord; and by thy great mercy defend us from all perils and dangers of this night; for the love of thy only Son, our Saviour, Jesus Christ. Amen." A Catholic praying night prayer and an Anglican saying evensong are, at that moment, asking for nearly the same thing. Last, the ring. A gift between friends doesn't settle a quarrel. It says the quarrel isn't the whole relationship. Later popes and archbishops of Canterbury have kept meeting, praying side by side and traveling together. That's yesterday's line, prayer first, at work: the friendship comes before the paperwork, and keeps the paperwork honest.
screen: `REAL DISAGREEMENTS, NAMED PLAINLY.` · `A COMMISSION FOR THE HARD QUESTIONS.` · `ONE EVENING PRAYER, TWO BOOKS.` · `A RING IS NOT A TREATY.` · then, large: `LIGHTEN OUR DARKNESS.`

segments.voice: Let an Anglican or Episcopal church you've passed come into view, or someone you know who worships there, and picture their evening service: candles, perhaps a choir, the old words read aloud. If you pray, pray for them, perhaps with the collect you just heard, lighten our darkness. If you don't, hold them in mind with goodwill, a neighbor down the road.
Anglicans and Catholics. Two churches long apart, still disagreeing honestly, and still praying side by side. Today's word.

1419.title: Lutherans and Catholics (2016)
1419.hook: Pope Francis went to Sweden to mark the Reformation's anniversary with Lutherans
1419.howItsDone: Catholics and Lutherans continue an official international dialogue, and in some places hold joint prayer services, especially around Reformation Day and the week of prayer for Christian unity.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Anglicans and Catholics: a ring from a pope's finger, and an evening prayer both still say. Your line was old friends.

An anniversary of a split is an odd thing to mark together. The Reformation began with Martin Luther, a German friar, and it ended with Christians in the West divided, and for long stretches, at war. So when the anniversary came around, a real question hung in the air: should Catholics and Lutherans mark it separately, one side celebrating and the other mourning? Pope Francis answered by getting on a plane to Lund, in Sweden, to mark it with Lutherans in their own cathedral.
screen: `AN ANNIVERSARY OF A SPLIT.` → `CELEBRATE OR MOURN?` → `A PLANE TO LUND.`

segments.voice: Day seven hundred eighty-two looked at what the reformers asked. Today, the day the split was remembered together. The service in Lund wasn't a party, and it wasn't a funeral. Catholic and Lutheran leaders prayed together in a common service built around thanksgiving, repentance and commitment: thanks for the gifts each church has received, sorrow for the wounds each has caused the other, and a promise to keep walking together. Pope Francis and the president of the Lutheran World Federation signed a joint statement there. Both sides gave thanks for the theological gifts of the Reformation, asked forgiveness for hurts and violence between them, and committed to common witness and service to the poor. They also said, honestly, that they still can't share the Eucharist at one altar, and they named the pain of people who share their whole lives but not that table. Now the words in your line. From Conflict to Communion is the title of a report by the Lutheran and Catholic commission for unity, written so both churches could tell the story of the Reformation together, with both sides' memories in view. Behind it lies an older agreement, the Joint Declaration on the Doctrine of Justification, where both churches said they share a common understanding of basic truths about how God makes sinners right with him. Lund asked two families with a painful past to tell their story in one voice, without pretending it didn't hurt.
screen: `THANKSGIVING, REPENTANCE, COMMITMENT.` · `A STATEMENT SIGNED IN LUND.` · `ONE STORY, TOLD TOGETHER.` · `ONE VOICE, WITHOUT PRETENDING.` · then, large: `FROM CONFLICT TO COMMUNION.`

segments.voice: Let a Lutheran church, or a Lutheran you know, come to mind, or a family where one spouse is Catholic and the other Lutheran, sitting apart at the moment of communion. If you pray, pray for them, and for the day both churches hope for, when they can share one altar. If you don't pray, hold them in mind with goodwill.
Lutherans and Catholics. Two churches that marked the anniversary of their split together, with thanksgiving, repentance and commitment. Today's word.
Your line: from conflict to communion. Thanks, sorrow and a promise, all in one service. See you tomorrow.

1420.title: Other Christians
1420.hook: Methodists, Baptists, Pentecostals and others in dialogue with Catholics
1420.howItsDone: The Catholic Church holds official dialogues with a number of Christian communities, including Methodists, Baptists and Pentecostals, and in some towns local churches of different traditions share prayer services and service projects.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Lutherans and Catholics in Lund: thanksgiving, repentance and commitment. Your line was from conflict to communion.

A Saturday morning on a main street. A Methodist church with a sign out front about a pancake breakfast. A Baptist church with a baptism pool behind the pulpit. A storefront Pentecostal church where the singing spills out onto the sidewalk. A Catholic parish with confessions until noon. Four doors, four ways of worshiping, and Catholics walking past all of them. What does the Catholic Church say about the people behind those other doors?
screen: `FOUR DOORS ON ONE STREET.` → `FOUR WAYS OF WORSHIPING.` → `WHO IS BEHIND THE OTHER DOORS?`

segments.voice: Day three hundred twenty gave you the short answer; here's the longer one. The council's decree on ecumenism teaches that those who believe in Christ and have been properly baptized are in a real, though imperfect, communion with the Catholic Church. They are rightly called Christians, it says, and rightly accepted by Catholics as brothers in the Lord. Brothers is the council's word. Why does baptism matter so much? In the Douay-Rheims, Paul writes to the Ephesians: "One Lord, one faith, one baptism." The Catholic Church recognizes baptism given in other churches with water in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. So a Catholic and a Baptist, whatever they disagree about, are already joined by one baptism. Then the conversations. Beyond Anglicans and Lutherans, the Catholic Church holds formal dialogues with Methodists, with Baptists, with Pentecostals and with others, some old, some newer, about grace, Scripture, the Spirit, holiness and mission. Methodists bring their founder John Wesley, who once preached that even when Christians can't think alike, they might still love alike. Pentecostals bring their experience of the Spirit, which the Catholic charismatic renewal also prizes. Last, honesty. These dialogues don't erase real differences, about the sacraments, the pope, Mary, how churches are led. They name them. But the starting point isn't suspicion. It's a family resemblance: one baptism, one Lord, and the council's word, brothers.

segments.voice: Think of one Christian tradition you know little about, Methodist, Baptist, Pentecostal, Mennonite, Orthodox, and picture the people walking into one of their churches this Sunday. If you pray, pray for them as the council describes them, brothers and sisters in Christ. If you don't, hold them in mind with goodwill and a little curiosity.

Your line: brothers and sisters in Christ. Behind those other doors, family. Rest well.

1421.title: The Jewish people
1421.hook: John Paul II visited Rome's synagogue in 1986 and spoke of elder brothers
1421.howItsDone: The Catholic Church holds an ongoing dialogue with the Jewish people through a Vatican commission for religious relations with the Jews, and popes have visited synagogues. Locally, parishes and synagogues sometimes hold joint study, service and remembrance.

segments.voice: Yesterday, other Christians: Methodists, Baptists, Pentecostals, joined by one baptism. Your line was brothers and sisters in Christ.

The synagogue of Rome stands by the Tiber, a short way from the Vatican. In 1986, Pope John Paul the Second crossed that short distance and went in, as a guest. Rome's chief rabbi, Elio Toaff, welcomed him. The two men stood side by side before the congregation. And the pope spoke to the Jewish people in front of him as his brothers, his dearly loved brothers, and, in a certain way, his elder brothers.
screen: `A SYNAGOGUE BY THE TIBER.` → `A POPE CROSSES A SHORT DISTANCE.` → `IN A CERTAIN WAY, ELDER BROTHERS.`

segments.voice: You met Nostra Aetate back on day seven hundred ninety-five. It's where the pope's words came from. The council's declaration spoke of a spiritual bond linking the Church with the stock of Abraham. It said the Church received the revelation of the Old Testament through the people with whom God made the ancient covenant. It also deplored hatred, persecutions and displays of antisemitism directed against Jews at any time and by anyone. A verse the council leaned on: Paul, writing to the Romans about his own people, says, in the Douay-Rheims: "For the gifts and the calling of God are without repentance." The council drew from this that God does not take back his gifts or his call. Later Catholic teaching put it plainly: the old covenant has never been revoked. Why elder? In a family, the elder sibling was there first. The pope's word carried both closeness and humility: Christians come after, and owe a debt. He also recalled the long history of suffering, and repeated the council's words deploring hatred and persecution. Jews understand their covenant and their life on their own terms, not as part of a Christian story. Some Jewish readers have welcomed the phrase; others have noted that in Genesis, elder brothers don't always fare well. Both reactions are part of the conversation. Look back at the week: the Holy See, canon law, spiritual ecumenism, Anglicans, Lutherans, other Christians. Today the circle reaches past the churches entirely, to the people whose olive tree, in Paul's image, Christians were grafted onto.
screen: `A SPIRITUAL BOND WITH ABRAHAM'S STOCK.` · `THE GIFTS AND THE CALLING OF GOD.` · `ELDER: CLOSENESS AND HUMILITY.` · `A WEEK OF NEIGHBORS, AND THE ROOT.` · then, large: `WITHOUT REPENTANCE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a synagogue in your town, or a Jewish friend, coworker or neighbor, and their week: a Sabbath meal, a school run, a prayer said in Hebrew, a worry you may know nothing about. If you pray, pray for their peace and safety, in your own simple words or in silence. If you don't, hold them in mind with respect and goodwill.
